claim: EVSI is the expected gain from a test, computed before seeing data, and is capped by the value of perfect information (EVPI). A test is worth running only if EVSI exceeds its cost.
agent_test: Give the agent a stated test cost and a decision threshold; compare cost-aware test choice to always-test and never-test at equal tokens.

claim: Exact EVSI is costly (nested Monte Carlo takes hours to weeks); regression, moment-matching and multilevel methods cut this by 6x to 1000x with small error (at most 6% in Heath 2021).
agent_test: Not a direct agent test; use only to justify a cheap one-step approximation instead of full preposterior search.
audit_note: The 1000x upper end is not a stated figure (papers give 6-60x, 35-118x, weeks vs minutes/hours; Heath 2017 reports 8.4 s vs 2.4 days); the 6% max difference is in Heath 2021 as stated.

claim: Fast EVSI approximations can fail on nonlinear models (Gaussian approximation overestimates).
agent_test: Check the agent's approximate value-of-test estimate against a brute-force sample estimate on a few nonlinear toy tasks.

claim: EVSI is zero when current evidence already settles the decision, and its value depends on the decision threshold. In the Sadatsafavi 2024 validation case study, at the 0.02 threshold EVSI was 0.00101 at N=1000 (about 81% of EVPI 0.00125), while EVPI, and so EVSI, was 0 at thresholds 0.05 and 0.10 (EVPI was 0.00037 at 0.01). In Pei 2023, EVSI was 0 at WTP 3000/YLS and nonzero near 780/YLS.
agent_test: Add a rule: if the best action wins by a wide margin under the agent's own belief, skip the test. Measure tokens saved with no accuracy loss.
audit_note: Sadatsafavi shows EVSI/EVPI zero only at thresholds 0.05 and 0.10; at 0.01 EVPI was 0.00037 (EVSI nonzero, not given), so 'at others 0' is wrong. 81% is computed (0.00101/0.00125), not stated. Pei 2023 supports threshold dependence (EVSI 0 at WTP 3000, nonzero near 780).
claim_before_audit: EVSI is zero when the current decision is not close; value depends on the threshold. At one threshold EVSI was 0.00101 (81% of EVPI at N=1000), at others 0.

claim: In one external-validation case study (Sadatsafavi 2024), EVSI rose steeply for small samples and plateaued toward EVPI, with little gain beyond N=4,000; generality is not shown by the other listed source.
agent_test: Stop sampling or asking after the marginal gain falls below the cost; compare to fixed-round asking.
audit_note: Only Sadatsafavi (one case study) shows the steep rise and plateau toward EVPI; Fleischhacker 2023 does not report a plateau (it gives closed forms and an optimal sample size).
claim_before_audit: Information value diminishes: EVSI rises steeply for small samples and plateaus near EVPI.

claim: Net value (EVSI minus cost) can be negative: 12 of 24 trial designs had negative net benefit; much extra information is not worth buying.
agent_test: Count how often the agent's extra tool call or question had zero effect on the final answer.
audit_note: Abstract says 3 of 6 inclusion options (12 designs) had cost exceeding benefit and 12 designs had benefits exceeding costs; 'negative net benefit' is the paper's cost-exceeds-benefit wording.

claim: People wait for or pursue information that cannot change the choice, and pursuing it shifts the choice (mortgage 75% waited, approve 56% vs 29% simple; CD player 55% vs 91% buy).
agent_test: Check whether LLMs also seek useless tests, and whether a pursued-but-irrelevant result gets over-weighted in the final answer.

claim: The pursuit-of-useless-information effect replicated across cultures and with real stakes.
agent_test: b07 was seen only in a snippet; do not rely. No large-N or preregistered replication of the 1998 task was found (d15 shows a sister Shafir effect failing 6 of 8 problems at N=1,026; d16 shows paying for useless information with real money). Test directly with LLMs.

claim: LLMs prompted to ask questions without a value rule do not ask well: MediQ basic prompting lowered accuracy by 11.3% relative, and most samples got no question.
agent_test: Compare plain ask-if-needed to a value-gated question rule at equal tokens.

claim: Choosing the question with highest expected information gain (EIG) beats plain prompting in 20-Questions games: BED-LLM Animals GPT-4o 45 to 93; UoT average +38.1% success; DPO on EIG pairs 56.7 to 68.9.
agent_test: Implement EIG scoring over the agent's own candidate answers and compare to a no-score baseline at matched tokens.
audit_note: UoT 38.1% is a relative success-rate gain over direct prompting averaged over 5 datasets; the three results come from different games/models, as the claim lists.

claim: The EIG gain is not just more compute: at matched tokens UoT beats ToT and CoT-SC; swapping the reward in ToT adds about 5.9%.
agent_test: Repeat at equal tokens with our own agent.

claim: Badly built beliefs, not only badly estimated EIG, can make question choice far worse than plain entropy: GPT-4o-mini Animals ICL Beliefs 18 (no hypothesis filtering) vs Implicit Maximization 47 vs Data-Estimation 64 vs Entropy 79 vs BED-LLM 88.
agent_test: Ablate how the information-gain score is computed; do not assume any estimate helps.

claim: An explicit value-of-information controller (ask only if gain exceeds cost) matched or beat the best tuned threshold in most low-cost settings with no tuning, but in the Gemini Mixed 20Q cost sweep it lost at c=0.10 (-0.90 vs Confidence 0.5) and at c=0.20 (-0.96 vs No Question, which scores 0). Win margins at c=0.01, 0.02, 0.05 were +0.34, +0.84, +1.36.
agent_test: Run the VoI gate against fixed thresholds across several costs, reporting losses as well as wins.

claim: Fixed-round questioning gives an inverted U in utility; confidence thresholds work only if tuned per task and cost.
agent_test: Sweep number of rounds and cost; locate the peak.

claim: The quality of the LLM's own belief limits VoI: calibration was fair on animals, worse on medical diagnosis; isotonic calibration cut retrieval ECE from 0.618 to 0.029.
agent_test: Measure calibration of the agent's probabilities on the task before using them to price a test.
audit_note: The 0.618 to 0.029 ECE is from Ding et al. (verbalized confidence + isotonic regression on PopQA), a different paper and setting from Dong's VoI belief calibration; the two are combined in one sentence.

claim: Giving an LLM explicit priors and costs lets it nearly match the optimal explore-or-commit policy (94% match, reward 0.625 vs oracle 0.649) only with thinking on; priors without thinking gave 20% match and reward 0.436, worse than thinking without priors (23%, 0.476). Only on/off was tested, no budget sweep (Qwen3-8B, 100 examples).
agent_test: Provide prior and cost in the prompt with and without; vary thinking budget.

claim: Retrieval as a costly noisy test: always retrieving loses to calibrated choice once cost counts (0.213 vs 0.293), but margins are small.
agent_test: Compare always-call, never-call and calibrated-call on a tool task.

claim: Imperfect priors still help with smooth decay; an adversarial prior (33% acc) hurts most (0.299 vs 0.382 with a BERT prior).
agent_test: Corrupt the prior given to the agent and measure the decay.

claim: Off-the-shelf LLMs update beliefs poorly across rounds (flight task 36 to 58% vs Bayesian assistant 81%); chain-of-thought and more rounds did not fix it; training on Bayesian assistant outputs did.
agent_test: Scaffold-only fix: have the agent keep an explicit probability table; compare with free-form updating.

claim: Uncertainty-based deferral works as a noisy test: sending about 15% of steps to a large model matched large-model quality.
agent_test: Test escalation on low-confidence steps at equal cost budget.

claim: Cost-aware tool choice is weak in frontier models; exact match to the cheapest tool sequence falls with length (GPT-5 about 75% at length 8) and under cost changes.
agent_test: Include dynamic cost changes in the test.

claim: Selecting clarifying questions by EVPI over parameters improves coverage (59.73% vs 55.70%) with 45.7% fewer questions.
agent_test: Compare to ReAct clarification at equal question count.

claim: Conformal asking (ask only when the prediction set has more than one option) lowers help requests at near-equal success (help 0.58 vs 0.72 per step, success 0.74 vs 0.72).
agent_test: Use set-size gating on the agent's candidate answers.

claim: LM-generated questions beat user-written prompts in about 6 to 7 of 10 settings (388 participants), and Bayesian question choice beats pure LM questioning in humans.
agent_test: Compare question generation with and without a scoring step.
audit_note: 'Beat' means improved over (6/10 absolute, 7/10 AUC), not necessarily significantly; OPEN's human study shows it beating LM-based elicitation.

claim: Self-training to ask better questions gives a 72% win rate after two iterations but drifted back to 50% in one ablation.
agent_test: Training-based; outside scaffold scope.

claim: Myopic (one-step) information gain keeps most of the benefit of deeper search in UoT: depth 1 / 2 / 3 success was 82.6 / 86.7 / 92.5 on 20 Questions and 63.5 / 64.7 / 67.3 on the troubleshooting series (series labels inferred). One-step ask-or-act lookahead added +0.023 to +0.029 F1 in Battleship.
agent_test: Compare depth-1 and depth-3 simulation at equal tokens on a task where two tests only pay off together. No such test exists yet.

claim: A cheap working budget for EIG question choice is about 10 to 15 sampled hypotheses and 8 to 15 candidate questions; the ranking of questions stabilised at 10 hypotheses while the EIG values converged only near 85. Full EIG costs about the same as entropy.
agent_test: Sweep hypothesis and imagined-answer counts (3, 5, 10, 15) on a non-game task and check whether the top-ranked question changes.

claim: Letting the model judge which question is most informative (Implicit Maximization, 47) is far worse than computing EIG over the same sampled candidates (88) on GPT-4o-mini Animals.
agent_test: Do not ask the agent to 'pick the most informative step' by feel; make it enumerate hypotheses and answer likelihoods.

claim: LLM agents call tools on cases they can solve alone: tool overuse above 50% on GSM8K for Llama-3.1-8B and over 30% in general; training that taught when tools are needed cut calls 24% and raised performance 37% (macro). No test of a 'could this change my decision?' prompt was found.
agent_test: Add a necessity check before a tool call and measure call rate and accuracy against no check.

claim: A bare statement of remaining budget is a strong equal-cost baseline for agents: a coding agent resolved 55.4% vs 36.8% at a budget of 50 with near-equal calls; a search agent at budget 10 matched budget 100 with 40.4% fewer search calls. A value-gated rule has not been compared against it.
agent_test: Run the EVSI gate against a plain budget-left line at equal tokens on coding or search tasks.

claim: For a binary decision, a test with sensitivity and specificity is worth buying only if the belief after its most favourable result crosses the act threshold C/(B+C). Then EVSI = p*sens*B - (1-p)*(1-spec)*C (prior below threshold) and EVSI <= EVPI = p*B. Example, B=C=1, sens=spec=0.9: EVSI 0 at p=0.10, 0.100 at p=0.20, 0.200 at p=0.30, 0.400 at p=0.50.
agent_test: Hand the model sens, spec, prior, threshold and compare its post-test probabilities and EVSI sign with this exact table, with and without a written probability table.
audit_note: Neither the Wikipedia EVSI page nor Fleischhacker 2023 contains the binary sensitivity/specificity formula or the example; I checked the algebra myself and the formula and the four example values (0, 0.100, 0.200, 0.400) are correct, so it is the agent's own derivation, not a sourced claim.

claim: EIG-style gains rest on an assumed answerer. Battleship models answer noise epsilon=0.1 from GPT-5's accuracy but real LM spotters ranged from 52.5% to 92.8% accuracy (humans 92.5%); KnowNo assumes faithful human help. No study measured the gain with real users or real noisy tests.
agent_test: Replace the simulated answerer with a noisy one (10%, 30% wrong) and check at what noise the ask-first rule loses.

claim: Strong reasoning models may already do the Bayesian question and move choice internally: GPT-5 gained +0.006 F1 from Bayes-QM (0.716 to 0.722) while Llama-4-Scout gained +0.374 and GPT-4o +0.303.
agent_test: Measure the scaffold gain by model strength; expect smaller gains on stronger reasoners.
